# Lead-Time Compression Without Quality Erosion: An Operations Plan

Fourteen weeks versus six is rarely a building-speed problem. It's a waiting problem. And the warranty spike from the last attempt tells you exactly what *not* to do: they compressed the work, including the quality work. The governing rule for this plan:

> **Compress the queue, never the gate.** The time isn't in the inspections — it's in the waiting *between* them. Cut touch time and you get defects. Cut queue time and you get speed. The last attempt confused the two; this plan is built on separating them.

The competitor quoting six weeks almost certainly isn't building faster. They've decoupled: pre-engineered modules, pre-certified designs, components on the shelf, assembly-to-order. **They start building before you start selling.** That's the real gap.

---

## 1. Where the 14 Weeks Actually Go

Before changing anything, run a four-week **order autopsy**: pull the last 25–30 shipped orders and reconstruct timestamped histories across every stage. In businesses like this, the findings are remarkably consistent:

| Stage | Elapsed time | Actual work | What's really happening |
|---|---|---|---|
| Quote → clean order release | 1.5–2.5 wks | 2–3 days | Incomplete specs at PO; sales↔engineering ping-pong; weekly release batching |
| Engineering & detailing | 2–3 wks | 3–5 days | Every order treated as custom; redraws; customer approval loops |
| Procurement (critical path) | 4–6 wks | — | Long-lead castings, drives, controls ordered *only after* release |
| Fabrication & machining | 3–4 wks | 5–8 days | Batch-and-queue; high WIP; expediting chaos |
| Assembly & wiring | 1.5–2 wks | 4–6 days | Starved by missing parts; waits on upstream batches |
| Inspection, test, documentation | 2–3 wks | 2–4 days | Inspector queue; third-party witness scheduling; certification package assembled *after* test |
| **Total** | **~14 wks** | **~3 wks touch time** | **~11 weeks is queue, handoff, batching, and rework** |

Three implications:

1. **There's a free 4–5 weeks available** from queue removal alone — no quality risk whatsoever.
2. **The inspections aren't the problem; the queues around them are.** An inspection takes hours. Waiting for the one certified inspector takes days. Assembling the documentation package retrospectively takes a week.
3. **Part of the 14 is padding.** Each function inflates its buffer because it doesn't trust the others. The blame game is literally priced into the quote.

---

## 2. Why the Last Attempt Failed — and the Rule That Prevents a Repeat

Post-mortem the warranty spike honestly. In nearly every case like this, the compression came from some combination of: shortened test durations, skipped in-process checks, drawings released incomplete ("fix it on the floor"), and documentation that lagged the build. Defects escaped and surfaced at customer sites.

Codify the lesson as a screening test applied to every proposed change:

- **Does it touch gate content** — what's inspected, test duration, hold points, witness requirements? → **Off the table.**
- **Does it touch only the queue, batching, or documentation lag around the gate?** → **Fair game.**

This single distinction is what makes the plan sellable to a burned quality organization.

---

## 3. The Changes: Process, Inventory, Scheduling, Supplier

| Lever | Change | Time impact |
|---|---|---|
| **Process** | **Configure-to-order platform:** rules-based design where ~80% of orders are pre-engineered standard modules + defined options; engineering-by-exception only | Engineering: 2–3 wks → 2–3 days on standard configs |
| **Process** | **Clean order entry:** no PO accepted without complete spec checklist; single customer approval point | –0.5–1 wk |
| **Process** | **Documentation-as-you-go:** digital traveler; material certs, weld logs, NDT reports scanned and compiled during the build, not after test | –1 wk |
| **Process** | **Inspection upstream:** in-process checks, first-article inspection, SPC — final gate becomes *confirmation*, not *discovery* | –0.5–1 wk of rework loops; protects quality |
| **Process** | **Daily material review board** (vs. weekly) with capped rework loops | –0.5 wk |
| **Inventory** | **Strategic stock of the top 10–15 long-lead items** (castings, drives, controls) against forecast | –3–5 wks off critical path |
| **Inventory** | **Component standardization** across the line — pooled demand makes stocking cheap and cuts unique-part count | Enables the above |
| **Inventory** | **Module supermarkets:** standard subassemblies built to stock; assembly starts day one | –1–2 wks |
| **Scheduling** | **Finite-capacity scheduling; schedule the constraint first** (usually test bays, certified welders, certified inspectors); promise dates generated from the schedule, not a blanket 14 | Kills the padding tax |
| **Scheduling** | **WIP caps (CONWIP) + smaller transfer batches.** Little's Law: lead time = WIP ÷ throughput. Halve WIP, halve flow time | –1–2 wks |
| **Scheduling** | **Standing slots for third-party witness points and FAT** instead of scheduling per order | –0.5–1 wk |
| **Scheduling** | **Level loading; end the quarter-end surge** that wrecks flow and forces re-padding | Stabilizes the quote |
| **Supplier** | **Blanket POs + rolling forecasts** to key suppliers; call-offs instead of fresh orders | Converts 6-wk supplier lead times to days |
| **Supplier** | **Supplier certification → dock-to-line:** certified suppliers skip incoming inspection queue | –0.5 wk |
| **Supplier** | **VMI/consignment** for standard items; frame agreements or dual-sourcing on true long-lead items | Risk reduction |

Note the sequencing logic: Phase 1 levers (queues, scheduling, stock, documentation) buy you 14 → 9–10 weeks with zero product change. Matching six weeks requires the modular platform — that's Phase 2.

---

## 4. Protecting the Quality Gates

Quality's fear is legitimate — they lived through the warranty spike. The plan gives them structural protection, not promises:

- **Non-Negotiable Gates Charter**, signed by all three function heads: gate content, hold points, witness requirements, and test durations are untouchable. **Quality holds veto power over gate content — full stop.**
- **Quality owns WHAT is inspected; Operations owns WHEN and how long the queue is.** Quality cannot be scheduled around, but inspection can be scheduled *like production* — inspectors and witness points get slots on the master schedule, not a queue.
- **Detection moves upstream.** In-process checks and SPC catch defects where they're cheap. The final gate stops being an archaeological dig.
- **Engage the certification body in Phase 0.** Pursue type-approval of standard modules and pre-approved quality plans, so per-order certification becomes *verification of a certified system* rather than a fresh event. Most certifiers welcome this — it's less repetitive work for them too.
- **Tripwires:** first-pass yield per gate, in-process escape rate, and documentation cycle time are published weekly. If any quality indicator flickers, compression pauses automatically — pre-agreed, no debate required.
- **Convert the trauma into a checklist.** The specific shortcuts that caused the warranty spike are documented and banned by name.

---

## 5. Aligning Production, Quality, and Sales

The feud is a KPI design problem. Each function is locally optimized and rationally blaming the others. Fix the scoreboard:

| Function | Old metric (drives blame) | New shared metrics |
|---|---|---|
| Sales | Bookings | Bookings **+ spec completeness at PO + quote-to-promise accuracy** |
| Production | Utilization / efficiency | **Flow time, WIP cap adherence, schedule adherence** |
| Quality | Escapes only | Escapes **+ inspection turnaround time + documentation cycle time** |

Critically, **quality gets measured on speed too** — so it stops being the consequence-free blocker — while escapes remain its veto metric.

Governance:

1. **One end-to-end owner.** Appoint an order-to-delivery value stream manager with authority across all three functions. Lead time currently has no owner; that's why no one is responsible for it.
2. **One shared scoreboard**, reviewed weekly by all three heads: quoted lead time, actual lead time, on-time delivery, first-pass yield, escapes. Same numbers, same room.
3. **Weekly S&OE meeting:** sales brings the 12-week demand picture, production commits capacity, quality commits inspector and witness coverage. Monthly S&OP ties the demand signal to strategic stock levels.
4. **Pilot first.** One high-volume product family, 90 days, co-designed by all three functions. Target: 14 → 9 weeks with zero change to gate content. Publish the before/after. The story — *"we took five weeks out and didn't touch a single gate"* — is what converts the skeptics.
5. **Fix the commercial side.** Sales quotes standard configurations from the configurator at real promise dates; free-form custom goes to a separate ETO lane with honest (longer) lead times and ETO pricing. Certainty is sellable — many customers will take a reliable 7 over a promised 6 that slips.

---

## 6. Roadmap and Expected Trajectory

| Phase | Timeline | Key actions | Quoted lead time |
|---|---|---|---|
| **0: Diagnose** | Wks 1–4 | Order autopsy, value stream map, baseline metrics, Gates Charter signed, certifier engaged | 14 (unchanged) |
| **1: Remove the queues** | Wks 5–16 | Inspection scheduling, digital traveler, daily MRB, WIP caps, clean order entry, strategic stock POs placed | **9–10 wks** |
| **2: Decouple** | Months 4–9 | Modular platform + pre-certification, supplier programs, finite scheduling live | **6–7 standard / 10–12 custom** |
| **3: Sustain** | Months 9–18 | Assemble-to-order at scale; monitor warranty-leading indicators 2+ quarters before declaring victory | **6 wks standard, matched to competitor** |

**The business case writes itself:** recovering even a fraction of the one-in-three deals lost on delivery dwarfs the cost of strategic inventory, two additional certified inspectors, and a value stream manager.

---

## 7. What Could Kill It

- **Forecast risk on stocked components** → start narrow (top families only), standardize parts to pool demand, govern through S&OP.
- **Certifier resistance** → engage in Phase 0, not Phase 2; frame as a certified system, not corner-cutting.
- **Sales keeps selling free-form custom** → the configurator carries the fast quote and the fast delivery; custom pays for itself.
- **Quarter-end pressure breaks WIP discipline** → requires explicit executive sponsorship; this is where past efforts quietly die.
- **"We tried this before"** → the charter, the tripwires, and the pilot exist precisely to answer that. Last time squeezed the gates. This time squeezes the queues — and quality co-signed the difference.

The end state isn't just a six-week quote. It's a company where the quote is *believable* — because production, quality, and sales are finally reading from the same schedule.
